newsitem.title: EGYPT: U.S. aid flap raises Egyptian hackles.
newsitem.headline: U.S. aid flap raises Egyptian hackles.

text.p: Egypt's hackles have been raised by the biggest challenge yet to the steady flow of U.S. aid that underpins the long relationship between the two countries.

Egypt and the United States have been close partners in Middle East diplomacy since President Jimmy Carter brought Egypt and Israel together at Camp David 19 years ago to hammer out the most enduring Arab-Israeli agreements ever signed.

One of the payoffs for Egypt was about $2 billion a year in U.S. aid -- money that helped the Egyptian government feed the urban poor and rebuild the country's infrastructure after decades of war with the Jewish state.

So when the U.S. Senate Appropriations Subcommittee on Foreign Operations failed to earmark aid to Egypt last week, it seemed in Cairo that the whole U.S. establishment had ungratefully turned its back on an old friend.
To add insult to injury, the committee did allocate Israel's standard annual instalment, defying the unspoken rule that any aid cuts should hit both countries equally.
The State Department, which would be free to provide aid to Cairo from the rest of the U.S. foreign aid budget, has stood by its request for more than $2 billion in aid to Cairo.

But in a country where parliament tamely endorses government policy, it will take some time for the Egyptian public to abandon the notion that the Senate committee was acting on some secret agenda set by the U.S. administration.
The gesture has put the Egyptian government right on the defensive, anxious to dispel any notion that it is vulnerable to economic aid deployed as a diplomatic weapon.
In a characteristic tough guy-soft guy approach, government papers have taken a defiant tone while ministers make reassuring noises about the durability of the U.S.-Egyptian relationships.

"The Senate subcommittee issued its decision based on blind bias to Israel that pays no regard to objective facts nor even to the interests of the United States itself," said the state-owned newspaper al-Akhbar in a front-page commentary.

"The fingers behind this senator (committee chairman Mitch McConnell) and the position of his subcommittee are not at all hidden but are clear and exposed for all to see. He must know that Egypt has been subjected to many pressures in its history but it never gave in and it never will," it added.

Foreign Minister Amr Moussa has pointed out the discrepancy between the views of the U.S. administration and those of the committee, which accused Egypt of obstructing talks between Israel and the Palestinians and "cosying up" to Libya, which is on Washington's list of pariah nations.
The government's other tack is to play down the significance of the aid, which has indeed declined in importance with inflation and with real economic growth in Egypt.
The money now represents about three percent of Egyptian gross domestic product, against about 12 percent in 1979.

"The Egyptian economy is strong and is growing fast and steady. It would not be greatly affected if U.S. aid is cut or abolished, since it is largely self-sufficient," Economy Minister Nawal el-Tatawi told reporters on Sunday.
But that argument may backfire, diplomats say. "The Egyptians would be unwise to shout that out too loud. Someone in Washington might hear them," one Western diplomat said.

For opposition politicians, a vocal group with little influence on events, the flap over aid is another opportunity to attack U.S. policy in the Middle East, and indirectly the government's connivance in Washington's dominant role.

"The Egyptian people cannot stand at the gates of the U.S. administration begging alms from Israel's agents in the White House, the Pentagon and the State Department, where the Jews are squatting," said the opposition newspaper al-Wafd.
"America's and Israel's dollars can go to hell," it added.
The opposition has also challenged the value of the U.S. aid, saying most of it goes on U.S. goods which Egypt does not need and on fees to highly paid U.S. consultants.
But analysts say that possibly the most important aspect of the aid, often overlooked, is the invisible subsidy to the Egyptian armed forces, about one half of the total.
Throughout the long peace which Egypt has enjoyed, the military aid has helped maintain the living standards and buy the loyalty of army officers, they say.
